newsitem.title: USA: TWA seen as unlikely acquisition target.
newsitem.headline: TWA seen as unlikely acquisition target.

text.p: As speculation mounts about the future of Trans World Airlines Inc, the financially strapped carrier seems an unlikely target for a takeover.

With many U.S. airlines posting record profits, TWA is heading in the opposite direction. It has an ageing fleet, no permanent chief executive and lots of debt. To make matters worse, it is facing tough contract negotiations with its unions this year.
"Why would someone want to buy TWA with their old aircraft and lousy hub?" said Stepehn Klein, an analyst with Standard & Poors Equity Group.
"They don't really bring anything. TWA needs to be rescued. But no one needs them to grow," Klein said.

On Friday, TWA denied an article in the newspaper USAToday, saying its board had met with investor Brian Freeman. The newspaper reported on Thursday that Freeman's Strategic Capital Group and Russian airline Transaero were seeking to take control of TWA.
Earlier TWA said it talked to "a number of different airlines about a number of different things" but declined to comment further about those discussions.

Often cited as the last "fixer-upper" in the U.S. airline industry, TWA would represent a liability to any carrier that might acquire it. Most other U.S. airlines have spent years repairing their balance sheets, analysts said.
Other industry experts also question TWA's long-term survival.
TWA's most valuable asset is its St. Louis hub, but it would not represent a benefit to most carriers because it would divert traffic from any acquirer's existing Midwest hub, analysts said.

TWA's low labor costs would not be an attraction either, analysts said. TWA's labor costs, about 30 percent below the industry average, would likely rise to levels at the acquiring airline, adding extra long-term costs for any suitor.
TWA has five labor contracts coming up for renewal this year, making it a likely target for growing labor unrest within the airline industry, analysts said.
TWA's fleet is older than that of any other major U.S. carriers, with an average age of 18.6 years, compared with the industry average of about 11.9 years.
TWA is also floundering without a permanent chief executive, and industry sources said the airline is not close decision.
TWA's board addressed the CEO situation at the board meeting on Tuesday, but "no announcement came from that meeting," TWA spokesman Mark Abels said.
